transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi Dr. Smith. Um, well, what brings me in is that I just can’t keep my words in a straight line anymore. Like, I'll start talking to someone about an overnight shift at work, and then I somehow end up jumping to soccer, and then paint colors, and then patient charts. I just... I can see everyone getting lost when I try to talk to them.
Over the past week or so, have you noticed your mood feeling unusually high, euphoric, or irritable, along with having much more energy than usual?

No, I haven't really felt high or euphoric. And I wouldn't say I have more energy than usual. If anything, I've just been feeling... really low and drained lately. I'm not irritable or hyper, just tired.
Have you been experiencing anything like hearing voices, seeing things others don't see, or having beliefs that others tell you aren't true?

I haven't heard voices or seen things that aren't there. But... about that last part. I'm sure the supervisors at work changed my shifts on purpose. I know they watch me through the unit cameras to see if I’m unsafe. People keep telling me it’s just because of staffing shortages, but... I know they're watching me.
How long have you been experiencing this combination of disorganized thinking, the belief that you're being watched, and your low mood — has it been days, weeks, or months?

It's been longer than that, actually. It's been going on for about a year and five months. It all started after my job switched my schedule around. I used to have steady day shifts, but then they put me on rotating nights and started giving me a lot of overtime. That's when I first started noticing all of this.
Have you noticed the belief that you're being watched or the trouble organizing your thoughts happening even during times when your mood wasn't low or drained?

Yeah, actually. There was a stretch of a few weeks where I wasn't in that deep depressed place. I felt mostly okay for a bit. But... I still knew they were watching me. I still believed the cameras and the supervisors were monitoring everything I did, so I just kept acting really guarded at work. The low mood lifted for a little while, but that feeling of being watched never stopped.
Over this past year and five months, have you noticed your ability to keep up with work duties, relationships, or daily responsibilities getting significantly worse because of these experiences?

Yeah, it really has. At work, I've... I've had to ask my coworkers to double-check my rounds and my charting. I just can't keep up with it on my own anymore. And at home, it's... it's pretty bad. I've fallen way behind on my bills, I've been completely ignoring my friends, and my apartment has just gotten completely out of control. 

It actually got bad enough recently that employee health stepped in. They sent me for an emergency evaluation because... well, I admitted to them that I was thinking about suicide.

Looking back over this whole year and five months, would you say the low, drained mood has been present for most of that time, or has it only come and gone for shorter stretches while the belief about being watched stayed constant throughout?

Looking back... yeah, that heavy, empty mood has been there for most of this whole period. Just this total loss of interest in everything. It's been going on for the majority of the time, actually. Even during the stretches when the worries about the cameras or my scattered talking were a bit quieter, that low feeling was still there. It's just been a constant weight for almost the whole year and five months.

latest_inference.note: Mood symptoms (depressive) have been present for the majority of the 1-year-5-month illness course, while psychotic symptoms (paranoid delusions, disorganized speech) persisted even during a period of a few weeks without depressive symptoms. This pattern—mood episode present for most of the illness duration plus psychosis persisting outside mood episodes—fits schizoaffective disorder, depressive type, and rules out schizophrenia (F20.9), which requires psychotic symptoms to predominate without a substantial mood component.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient exhibits persistent psychotic symptoms (persecutory delusions of being watched/monitored) and disorganized speech that continued even during a period of weeks when depressive mood was absent, satisfying the criterion for psychosis independent of mood episodes. However, depressive symptoms (low, drained mood, anhedonia, suicidal ideation) have been present for the majority of the total illness duration (~17 months), fulfilling the mood component criterion for schizoaffective disorder. The overall presentation, combining significant functional decline, chronicity exceeding a month, and predominance of depressive mood alongside persistent delusions, best fits Schizoaffective Disorder, Depressive Type (F25.1) rather than pure Schizophrenia (psychosis without mood predominance) or Major Depressive Disorder with psychotic features (which would require psychosis only during mood episodes).
